newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz boosted in anti-Islamist quest.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz boosted in anti-Islamist quest.

text.p: Turkish secularist hope Mesut Yilmaz, boosted by an opponent's defection, pledged on Sunday to make the most of his opportunity of keeping resurgent Islamists out of power by becoming the country's next prime minister.
"We now have a chance to end the crisis which the government has brought this country into," Yilmaz told supporters at a rally in Istanbul.
Motherland Party leader Yilmaz was nominated prime minister-designate last Friday in a bid to replace the Islamist-led coalition of Necmettin Erbakan, who resigned under pressure from the military.
He does not yet have the numerical support in parliament to form a government of his own but NATO member Turkey's secularist elite is rooting for him.
"If we want to pass on a powerful and prosperous country to our children, now is the time for working together," Yilmaz told a crowd of around 300 people.
"The way to get more powerful is to unite against our enemies," said Yilmaz, a staid conservative who has had two brief spells as prime minister this decade.
He has given himself until the end of this month to secure enough backing for a right-left alliance that could win a confidence vote in parliament.
His main rival for the top job is Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, formerly Turkey's first woman prime minister who is allied with Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party.

A dissident MP from Ciller's True Path Party quit on Sunday, giving Yilmaz a lift. "Deputy Haluk Muftuler's resignation reached the parliamentary speaker's office in the early hours of this morning," the NTV television news channel said.
The resignation reduced the number of MPs in the pro-Islamic front backed by Ciller to 281. Yilmaz said the rebel deputy would join his Motherland Party on Monday.
Yilmaz can only count on a maximum of 266 votes in the 550-seat parliament, but he was confident of further defections from among anti-Islamist dissidents in Ciller's party.
"In the days ahead we expect more resignations although I cannot give a figure, " Anatolian news agency quoted him as saying.
A handful of Ciller's members have said publicly they will no longer support a government that includes the Islamists.

Erbakan had been in coalition with Ciller for the last year. He angered the secularist generals and some of his government allies with proposals for mild Islamist reforms, like lifting a ban on women civil servants wearing Islamic headscarves to work.
Erbakan stepped down in the hope that President Suleyman Demirel would give Ciller the mandate to form a new alliance with the Islamists and then go for early elections.
The president defended himself against criticism by the Islamist alliance that he should have nominated Ciller to forge a government because she has the support of more MPs.
"There is nothing wrong. Everything is correct and in line with the constitution," Turkish television quoted Demirel as saying on Saturday night.
"I don't want to get involved in an argument. If I start arguing, there will really be trouble," he said.
Demirel has the authority to appoint his own government and call early polls if Yilmaz fails to win a confidence vote.
